title: Κόραξ καὶ ὄφις
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 167. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κόραξ τροφῆς ἀπορῶν, ὡς ἐθεάσατο ὄφιν ἔν τινι εὐηλίῳ τόπῳ κοιμώμενον, τοῦτον καταπτὰς ἥρπασε.
sentences.tr: Korax trophēs aporōn, hōs etheasato ophin en tini euēliōi topōi koimōmenon, touton kataptas hērpase.
sentences.l: A raven, being at a loss for food, when he saw a snake sleeping in a certain sunny place, having flown down snatched it up.
sentences.i: A raven hard put to find food saw a snake asleep in a sunny spot, and swooped down and snatched it up.
sentences.n: ἀπορέω takes the genitive of what one lacks: τροφῆς ἀπορῶν, "at a loss for food". ἐθεάσατο … κοιμώμενον is a supplementary participle — a verb of perceiving takes a participle for what is seen happening, where a verb of saying would take an infinitive. καταπτάς is the aorist participle of καταπέτομαι, "fly down"; the aorist-participle chain (saw … flew down … snatched) is the ordinary engine of these fables.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ ἐπιστραφέντος καὶ δακόντος αὐτόν, ἀποθνῄσκειν μέλλων, ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε δείλαιος, ὅστις τοιοῦτον ἕρμαιον εὕρηκα ἐξ οὗ καὶ ἀπόλλυμαι. »
sentences.tr: Tou de epistraphentos kai dakontos auton, apothnēiskein mellōn, ephē· « All’ egōge deilaios, hostis toiouton hermaion heurēka ex hou kai apollymai. »
sentences.l: But it having turned about and bitten him, he, being about to die, said: « But I for my part am wretched, I who have found such a windfall from which I am also destroyed. »
sentences.i: But when the snake turned and bit him, he said, as he lay dying: « Wretched creature that I am, to have found such a godsend, and to be destroyed by it. »
sentences.n: Τοῦ δὲ ἐπιστραφέντος καὶ δακόντος is a genitive absolute: a noun and participle set in the genitive to give the attendant circumstance, with no grammatical link to the main clause — English wants "when…". ἕρμαιον is a windfall, a piece of luck credited to Hermes, patron of lucky finds; it is precisely the word that makes the raven's death ironic. ὅστις, the indefinite relative, carries a causal colour here — "seeing that I have found". εὕρηκα is perfect (the find stands) against the present ἀπόλλυμαι (the ruin is under way). No copula is written with δείλαιος; ἐστί is left out, as constantly.

sentences.t: Οὗτος ὁ λόγος λεχθείη ἂν ἐπ’ ἄνδρα ὃς διὰ θησαυροῦ εὕρεσιν καὶ περὶ σωτηρίας ἐκινδύνευσεν.
sentences.tr: Houtos ho logos lechtheiē an ep’ andra hos dia thēsaurou heuresin kai peri sōtērias ekindyneusen.
sentences.l: This story might be told of a man who, through the finding of a treasure, ran a risk even concerning his life.
sentences.n: λεχθείη ἄν is the potential optative — aorist passive optative with ἄν, the hedged "might be told". The same closing elsewhere in the collection takes ἐπί with the genitive; Chambry prints the accusative here. κινδυνεύω περί + genitive is to run a risk over something, and σωτηρία is bare survival, not salvation. καί is "even": the treasure cost him not merely trouble but his life.
